Name: -1_did_performance_guy_thoughts
Representative_Docs: ['I tried not to think about the speech task too much afterward, as I knew I could not change  the evaluators’ impressions of me and my performance and I found it stressful to reflect on it. I was mostly successful in thinking of other things, but when it did come to mind, I mostly considered what the evaluators might have thought about my performance and how it compared to other people completing the same task. I also thought about the implications of the speech task outside of the study; though performing badly in this task had no direct impacts on other aspects of my life, it reminded me that this type of task is something I struggle with in general, and I was concerned about the possibility of having to do a similar task in a setting that would have more real consequences for me.', "My thoughts haven't changed at all since yesterday. While I did respond to the earlier questions about their perception of me based on their facial expressions and body language, I suspect that each of the evaluators were instructed beforehand to be dismissive/affirming/neutral; their expressions during my speech may not have been indicative of their true thoughts. As for my speech itself, I thought I did reasonably well in describing my dream job, except perhaps a bit of rambling towards the end.", "I thought it was a fun experience overall. Being told to try to keep my hands still prior to the start of the speech gave me a bit of anxiety because it's hard to focus on not using my hands while talking. Other than that, I thought it was fine. I can ramble. Could I have been more eloquent in my delivery? Certainly. Though why try to be perfect when that's an impossible task? The expectation of being liked and perceived well by everyone is anxiety inducing in itself. If others do not like me or judge me negatively, it's normal. I dislike some people and I judge others. Everyone does. It's pointless to worry about each impression one makes. Some people will like you, and that should be enough. I remember laughing after the evaluators left. Focusing on being still while attached to wires did give me slight anxiety. I could tell the middle guy was relatively neutral. The left guy and right guy basically swapped their mannerisms. Left was disengaged at first, yet he was engaged at the end. Right did the opposite. In the end, it doesn't matter what they thought of me."]

Name: 0_evaluators_middle_evaluator_nervous
Representative_Docs:
['I keep thinking about how they were acting. The middle evaluator seems very approachable at the beginning. They were the ones that basically said hello and this is what we’re doing et cetera and they were the only ones that talked. As I tried to go about my speech, I noticed that their eyes were locked on me and there was no emotion or expression on their face so that made me really nervous and then the evaluator on the left was bouncing his leg and looking at his watch and the one on the right was shaking his head vigourously and at some point during the speech the left and right change their behaviours. They just switched them out so the one on the right was looking at his watch slouching back in his chair and almost saying like are you done yet and then the one on the left was shaking his head but the one in the middle remained steadfast and was staring me down.  I was very very nervous and I could barely even talk or focus because I was so focused on what they were doing and how they were looking at me and the way they were acting.', 'For the first hour or two after leaving the lab, I thought about the evaluators' body language and facial expressions. The assumption I made when seeing their photo at the beginning was completely different from what I felt when seeing them in person. The first time I saw them in person, they seemed a bit threatening. By the second time they came in for the speech, my assumptions about how they would react to me or my presentation had shifted entirely.
For example, the left evaluator seemed very attentive and interested. The middle evaluator was quite critical and judgmental, while the right evaluator started out as interested but seemed to stop paying attention at some point. These are actually the exact types of responses I usually get whenever I discuss my work, so I wasn't very surprised.
Still, seeing that two out of the three seemed critical or uninterested made me feel like it would be better to cut the speech short. However, at that point, it was already at the three-minute mark.
It would also have made more sense and been more relatable if I had known why I was making the speech to them and who they were in connection with the outcome of the speech/study.
Overall, I'm glad I challenged myself to talk about my current work and passion. Initially, I thought about speaking about a hypothetical dream job, which would have been more of a fun, imaginary speech. I'm glad I chose the real one instead; it allowed me to display real feelings and expressions.
At the beginning, I heard my voice shaking and felt a bit nervous, even though my head was telling me that there was nothing to be nervous about. It is always a bit emotional to explain my work because it deals with global inequality, a topic that makes me and some people sad, while others react with, "It's not my problem," or shrug with disinterest. As a result, whenever I speak about my work, I have to remind myself to expect different reactions and accept that some people will try to be understanding and supportive, while others remain completely indifferent.
After a couple of hours, I stopped thinking about it completely. Overall, it was a positive challenge, and I'm happy I participated in and contributed to your research.', 'I recall my heart beating out of my chest during the 3 minute preparation section but that the beating became quiet when the evaluators re-entered the room. I felt I could share a convincing narrative of my dream job even with internal doubts I did not plan to share, nor did I share them, with the evaluators. The middle evaluator was calm and neutral, besides some smiles along the way. The left and right evaluators gave polar opposite signals and seemed to swap the signals at one point in the session. I don’t believe these signals impacted my performance though they did shift my attention momentarily if there was a strong movement like a nod or head shake. I felt more conscious that I talked with my hand or looked to the ceiling, the first of which was discouraged. I felt somewhat calmer after the task was completed, and I had some nervous laughter at the very end when removing the sternum tape because it tickled and hurt, though perhaps that opened me to be more expressive about the awkwardness of the evaluation. I felt mostly ok about this in the moment and after, both immediately and in the following day, because the weight of the evaluators’ evaluation is less consequential. I wonder how I might respond in a panel of future managers of mine at a dream company/position. I certainly do get nervous when presenting for my PhD.']

Or even if the interviewers were still all men, I would have been more comfortable with a woman still in the room.", "Mostly I keep cringing and yearning for death (I don't mean seriously) about how I came across on the study
But the questions seem to presuppose the problem was with my ability or self-concept; I didn't then and don't now feel stupid for what I said (or my inability to say it); I have always been awkward, and the setup of the task (so on the nose to make one self-conscious) I felt actually ended up relieving the worry. And I don't feel stupid for how I speak; speaking is one of the ways I can stave off feeling horrible. 
Instead, the study made me cringe endlessly, pains me now, because it connected up with preexisting problems with self-concept that I am hateable, pretentious, arrogant, etc., and also socially incompetent 
In many ways I wish I would have come across as more conventionally self-conscious, with awkward body language, because then I would at least meet with pity. Instead, I feel like I came across so strangely and arrogantly, and idiotically began to talk about the psychodynamics of graduate school or academic life, to an audience which could interpret it as insulting. 
So the self-consciousness and awful feelings are high, but they're not related specifically to ability; ability is all I have, and was so outwardly compromised by circumstances. Instead, self-consciousness manifested by latching onto preexisting agonies about the impossibility of being received right socially....
And everyone in the study was close in age to me too, both the evaluators and the person I interacted with who administered the study to me...."]

Name: 5_experiment_reaction_embarrassed_anxiety
Representative_Docs:
["I generally thought I should have done better, and decided I should think more about how I would pitch myself in the future. I did not dwell too much on what actually happened because I knew there was no pressure attached, though I did feel a bit self-conscious about how nervous I was during the task and because I felt I did not do very well. I also wondered about what the purpose of each evaluator's reaction was, and how if how I perceived them was how they were intended. I also realized that the stress of the exercise and thinking about what to say caused me to not pay them very much attention at times, which in real life would likely impact a panel's perception of me negatively. I thought mostly about how anxiety/stress impact me during presentations, because when I am put on the spot for speeches or even presentations that I am given more time to prepare for, I often black out a bit from anxiety where I forget what I plan to say and have little memory of anyone else. Because of this, I am generally unable to use presenter notes/exact scripts because they will trip me up more - instead I have to carefully prepare general thoughts I want to convey / important points and then I often end up improvising on the spot, (though visual assistance from slides is helpful to prompt me). In this scenario, it meant that I was unable to pay attention to both the presenters and their behavior very much, because I was focused on staying calm and speaking clearly, which also makes me quite uncertain what their impressions of me were.", 'I felt excited as well as anxious before the task. My heart rate was up before we start. The first 3 minutes I found myself thinking about what I’m gonna say and felt confident. Although when the evaluators got back to the room I forgot how to start.
During the task I got distracted but the evaluators reaction and I wasn’t anxious anymore. I felt anger and disrespect and tried to concentrate on the task which I couldn’t. I was thinking this is the challenge I am supposed to handle at the time, yet I was surprised and I couldn’t manage to focus. I tried to remind myself that this isn’t a real situation, and I’m being observed about it with my reaction which made it a bit funny, and it didn’t help with the focus at all. After the task while I was alone in the room I found myself thinking about the details, like how I avoided looking at the evaluators who were ignoring me while I was speaking and they changed their parts in turns and  smiled at me . I guess their smile after the ignorance was funny at first, but it felt disrespectful too. So I had this mixed feelings which was not pleasant. 
I was kind of disappointed that I didn’t manage the situation although I felt a bit happy and grateful for the experience. 
One other point I feel worth mentioning is that night I told my husband about the task and my feelings which he found me excited and happy about it. When I was telling him about my reactions, I mentioned that I was obligated not to move so much because of all the items attached to me and made me limited. Im kind of person who  talks with my hands and I wasn’t free to be myself enough. 
I felt more grateful for the experience the next day :) 
I hope it helps you with your research. Thanks for the experience.', 'The task felt like it was set up to trigger anxiety in participants, from the mechanics of placing the sensors, to some of the words in the word-matching task, to the mechanics of the mock-interview (three interviewers on one, all in a row, all men). I did think a number of times about this mistakes I made (repeating things I didn't mean to, not following the outline I tried to plan beforehand/talking-points coming out in a disorganized order, forgetting the word "instrumentation", voice too quiet, use of filler words, saying things that were not smart or that I felt embarrassed about) and felt bad about those. I did not feel bad about them because I thought a negative evaluation would mean there was something wrong with me, but I still felt embarrassed when I thought about my mistakes and my performance. In part because the setup of the experiment was inherently stressful (as outlined previously), in part for reasons that might be particular to me as a participant and were not general to the experimental setup. (There were elements of the experiment that primed me to think about a prior work experience involving an application/evaluator that was stressful for me, and I felt that most of my thoughts about the experiment after-the-fact stemmed from that internal connection rather than the experiment itself; I don't typically feel the same type of anxiety that I felt surrounding the experiment for real work presentations/tasks at my current job, which has genuine stakes.) I definitely felt like I had a stress-based physiological response during the task (quicker breathing, heart-rate, blood pounding), and that it took awhile afterward for that response to resolve.']
